rationale: B wins because it is more disciplined about what is blocked, what proof would unblock it, and which beat would actually care. Its line, "Without a timeframe the number is bare and this angle is a topic, not a story," is the adult in the room. A is strong, but "whether repair-and-resale is graduating from boutique perk to standard retail infrastructure" starts importing a market thesis before the evidence has earned it. B still needs one factual haircut, but it gives the founder sharper marching orders.
gaps_in_A: "whether repair-and-resale is graduating from boutique perk to standard retail infrastructure" stretches one Patagonia rollout into a category-maturity thesis before comparative data exists.
"Patagonia expands a program built to sell you less clothing" is a good contrarian line, but it leans too hard on intent the update does not prove.
"How to get Patagonia gear repaired for free now that it's in every store" over-promises free repairs when complex repairs are charged at cost, and it blurs US stores into every store.
The next step, "find-journalists," is a little premature before choosing which proof gaps can actually be filled.
gaps_in_B: "Patagonia puts a repair counter in every US store" invents a physical/operational detail. The update says drop-off is available, not that each store has a repair counter.
"what it costs to staff 70-plus locations for it" is a useful reporting question, but it risks implying in-store staffing the facts do not establish.
"Patagonia's newest store rollout has nothing new to sell" is punchy but too absolute; the update only says no new apparel line was announced.
"That reporter will write the story with or without your cooperation" is a bit performative. Useful warning, but it edges toward editor theater.
